title: The title promises, the first seconds prove
when: When writing a title and the opening of a video.
summary: The most viewed videos of all twelve channels promise a hidden truth ("the real reason", "the disturbing history", "why it looks weird") or a counted list ("7 principles"), and the first 5-15 seconds restate that promise as a question over the strongest picture the video has.
do: Restate the title's promise as a question in the first 5-15 s.
Open on the most striking picture of the story (the climax, the strangest detail, the face reacting), then rewind.
Pay the promise off visibly: the answer gets its own beat, not a passing line.
avoid: a slow context opening
a title promise the video never pays off
source: Study of 12 channels the owner named (2026-10-18): channel pages, Popular sort, durations and storyboard contact sheets of a typical video each (Vox, Johnny Harris, MagnatesMedia, Iman Gadzhi, Ali Abdaal, IMPERIAL, maximise, Metro Media House, LEMMiNO, kold / Sam Kolder, Arsacre, Gawx Art). Techniques only, in our own words; notes in docs/research/channel-study-2026-10-18.md.

title: One visual system per video
when: When planning the look of a whole video.
summary: Each strong channel builds a video from one recurring visual system (an illustrated world that comes back, a parchment map with flag pins, white line art on black with one red, floating evidence on black, a dark set with matching 3D icons); cutaways share the palette of the main picture.
do: Decide the video's system in the plan summary: its ground, its recurring device and its one accent.
Return to the same device when the story returns to its topic (a callback).
Make cutaways and graphics in the same palette as the main shots.
avoid: a different visual idea on every shot
graphics in colours the rest of the video never uses

title: Show the receipts
when: In documentaries, business stories and essays that make claims.
summary: The channels show their evidence: documents and headlines with a highlighted line, quote cards with a portrait and a name, screenshots, maps, archive photos, charts of the numbers they say.
do: When the script cites a source, show it: a document (with the line that matters lit), a quote card (portrait, name, words), a headline.
Use the words and numbers of the script only; label a reconstruction as such.
One piece of evidence per screen, held long enough to read.
avoid: fake real logos or mastheads
a quote the narration never says or attributes

title: Maps carry geography and power
when: Whenever a line names countries, routes, borders, wars, trade or influence.
summary: Geopolitics channels build whole chapters on maps: regions light up one at a time, routes sweep, pins drop, and networks of people and countries are drawn on the map.
do: Use a map for every place-driven claim, with one or two things lighting up per sentence.
Show influence as links between pins (who backs whom) or as coloured blocs.
Hold a map at least 3 s and fly the camera to the region being talked about.
avoid: a map flashed for a second
lighting up everything at once

title: Who connects to whom
when: When a story has several people, companies or countries acting on each other.
summary: Business and political stories become clear when the cast is drawn as a network: portraits or icons connected by labelled links that appear as the narration names each tie.
do: Use a network element (or pins and routes on a map) whose links draw on the words that name each relation.
Keep the same network and add to it as the story grows; return to it at the turn.
avoid: more than six nodes at once
a new layout for the network every time it returns

title: How often the picture changes, by format
when: When setting the pace of shots for a format.
summary: Observed picture changes on contact sheets: explainers and talking-head lists change every 3-5 s, story documentaries every 5-10 s with motion inside each shot, music-led films several times every 5 s on the beat, calm mysteries hold 6-10 s with slow motion inside.
do: Explainers and lists: a new shot or a new beat every 3-5 s.
Story documentaries: 5-10 s shots that each move inside (camera, arrivals, maps).
Mystery and investigation: long, quiet holds with slow pushes and evidence arriving one piece at a time.
Music-led films: cut on the beat, several cuts every 5 s.

title: Choose a narration mode on purpose
when: When writing or directing the narrator for a family.
summary: Each successful channel keeps one narration mode; choose one per family and keep it.
do: Curious explainer: a question, the mechanism, the consequence; plain words, second person.
First-person investigator: "let me show you", the research shown, personal stakes.
Dramatic storyteller: open at the climax, then rise and fall, tension in the pauses.
Direct list coach: numbered points, each a promise, a proof and an example.
Evidence teacher: named frameworks, studies cited, friendly and calm.
Dry historian: precise facts with an understated wit.
Calm mystery narrator: measured, sparse, long pauses before evidence.
avoid: imitating a real narrator's voice, catchphrases or name
switching mode inside a video
source: Study of 12 channels the owner named (2026-10-18): channel pages, Popular sort, durations and storyboard contact sheets of a typical video each (Vox, Johnny Harris, MagnatesMedia, Iman Gadzhi, Ali Abdaal, IMPERIAL, maximise, Metro Media House, LEMMiNO, kold / Sam Kolder, Arsacre, Gawx Art). title: Length follows the story
when: When choosing a target length for a video.
summary: Observed lengths: explainers 8-30 min, story documentaries 20-60 min, numbered lists 12-20 min, deep mysteries 30 min to over 2 h, short films 2-6 min. The story decides, never a fixed number.
do: Pick the target minutes from the format and the depth of the story.
Cut a long video into chapters that each re-hook.
Mid-roll ads start at 8 minutes; never pad a story to reach it, because lost retention costs more than the mid-roll earns.

title: The rise-and-fall saga
when: For business, empire and biography stories.
summary: Cold open at the climax, then: origin, the rise, the conflict, the fall or the twist, and the legacy. Each act ends on a question.
steps: Cold open: the most dramatic moment, then "but how did it get here?"
Origin: humble or strange beginnings, one vivid detail.
Rise: the clever move, with the numbers.
Conflict: the rival, the scandal, the law.
do: End every act on an open question.

title: The case file mystery
when: For unsolved cases, disappearances, codes and mysteries.
summary: Present the case, then the evidence one piece at a time, the theories with their weaknesses, what is actually known, and an honest open ending.
steps: The case in one striking image and one sentence.
Evidence, one piece at a time, each held and sourced.
Theories, each tested against the evidence.
avoid: presenting a theory as fact
invented evidence

title: The counted list
when: For numbered advice, lessons and principles.
summary: Each item is a promise, a proof and an example; a counter shows where the viewer is (item 3 of 7); the strongest item comes last or second to last.
do: Show the position with a dial or counter (gauge with steps).
Give each item a visual metaphor of its own.
Order items so the strongest lands late.
avoid: items of equal length and look
the best item first and a weak one last
